435.title: Bhagiratha and the rest of us
435.hook: a king whose grandfather and father both failed to bring the Ganga down doesn't stop, and Patanjali says why that matters
435.carry: faith and intensity, not talent, bring you near
435.tomorrow: an elephant's strength runs out. who comes?
435.howItsDone: In Hindi a vast, stubborn effort is still called a Bhagiratha effort, and yoga teachers often present shraddha, virya, smriti, samadhi and prajna as qualities anyone can cultivate, pointing to sutra 1.21 to say that sincere intensity matters more than natural gifts.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sabija, Arjuna seeing only the bird. Samadhi: the mind gathered on one seed. Today, who gets there, and how?
screen: `SAMADHI — THE MIND GATHERED ON ONE SEED.`

segments.voice: You met Bhagiratha on day one hundred fifteen: the king who brought the Ganga down from heaven. Here's the part before. Sixty thousand of his ancestors, the sons of King Sagara, lay burned to ash by the sage Kapila, and only the Ganga's water could free them. His grandfather, Anshuman, tried for the rest of his life and died without her. His father, Dilipa, worried over it and died without an answer. Nobody in that family was born able to do this. Then it was Bhagiratha's turn.
screen: `SIXTY THOUSAND IN ASHES.` → `A GRANDFATHER TRIED. A FATHER TRIED.` → `THEN BHAGIRATHA.`

segments.voice: In Valmiki's Ramayana, he hands his kingdom to his ministers and goes to Gokarna to practice tapas: arms raised, fires around him, eating once a month, for a very long time. Brahma grants the river, but warns that only Shiva can bear her fall. So Bhagiratha begins again, standing on the tip of one toe for a year, until Shiva agrees. In Hindi, a vast, stubborn effort is still called a Bhagiratha effort. Patanjali has words for what Bhagiratha had. Sutra 1.19 admits that a few beings reach deep absorption by their very nature; the commentator Vyasa adds that their state wears off, so they aren't the goal. Sutra 1.20 turns to everyone else: five things come first. Shraddha, faith, a settled trust that the path is real. Virya, energy. Smriti, memory, keeping the aim in view. Samadhi, the gathering. Prajna, wisdom. Talent isn't on the list, and each can be grown. Sutra 1.21: it is near for those whose urgency is intense. And 1.22 grades even that: mild, medium, intense. This is a real Hindu conviction, and the stories keep telling it: the goal isn't reserved for the born-holy. Many teachers read these sutras this way: how near you are depends on how much you care, not on what you were born with. Today, it might be a grandmother you assume was born devout, who in fact just kept getting up early.

segments.voice: If you pray, sit with a name of God you love; if you don't, with the breath. Touch the five, a few breaths each: faith, trusting that this sitting counts; energy, lengthen the spine and wake the body; memory, recall why you came. Then gather on the name or the breath. For wisdom, notice without judging how intense your wanting is today, mild, medium or intense. Any of them is a fine place to start.
Shraddha, faith, a settled trust that the path is real, the first of the five in sutra 1.20. Bhagiratha kept it after two generations of his family had failed.

436.title: Gajendra lifts a lotus
436.hook: an elephant king fights a crocodile until his strength is gone, and Patanjali's one small word, or, opens a second road
436.carry: ishvara pranidhana: a road met from the other side
436.tomorrow: Death gives a boy one word. which one?
436.howItsDone: Many Hindu yoga lineages treat ishvara pranidhana as central, practiced through prayer, offering one's actions to God and repeating a divine name, while others teach it as one of several supports for meditation; many Vaishnavas also recite Gajendra's prayer from the Bhagavata.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-THIRTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhagiratha: faith and intensity, not talent, bring you near. All that effort. Today, what happens when effort runs out.
screen: `FAITH AND INTENSITY, NOT TALENT.`

segments.voice: Gajendra is the king of the elephants. In the Bhagavata Purana he wades into a lake on Mount Trikuta with his herd, and a crocodile clamps onto his leg. He pulls. The crocodile pulls. His herd tries to help and can't. The fight goes on, the Purana says, for a thousand years, and the elephant, stronger on land, slowly loses to the crocodile in its own water. His strength is gone. And then Gajendra stops pulling, and starts to pray.
screen: `A CROCODILE IN THE LAKE.` → `A THOUSAND YEARS OF PULLING.` → `THEN HE PRAYS.`

segments.voice: He doesn't call on a particular god by name. He prays to the one who is the source and shelter of everything. The Bhagavata says that because the prayer named no single form, the other gods held back, and Vishnu himself came, riding Garuda. Seeing him, Gajendra lifts a lotus in his trunk as an offering, and the crocodile is cut away. You sang this rescue in the arti on day one hundred twenty. Patanjali has his own version of that turn. For twenty-two sutras he's talked like a coach: practice, let go, turn up the intensity. Then sutra 1.23: ishvara pranidhanad va. Or, by devotion to Ishvara. Va, or: a second road. Ishvara means the Lord. Pranidhana means setting yourself down before: devotion, surrender. The commentator Vyasa says that through this devotion the Lord turns toward the practitioner and favors them, and absorption comes near. The road is met from the other side. Like Gajendra, Patanjali names no particular god: sutras 1.24 to 1.26 call Ishvara a special seer, untouched by affliction and karma, all-knowing, the teacher of the most ancient teachers. Scholars debate how central this is; many Hindu lineages take it as a real call to bhakti. And that's the teaching: in Hindu devotion, surrender isn't giving up. Gajendra fought with everything he had, then let himself be helped. Today it's the moment you've tried your hardest and quietly say, I can't carry this alone.
screen: `NO NAME, AND VISHNU COMES.` · `PATANJALI'S OWN TURN.` · `VA: OR. PRANIDHANA: SURRENDER.` · `UNTOUCHED, ALL-KNOWING, THE FIRST TEACHER.` · then, large: `SURRENDER ISN'T GIVING UP.`

segments.voice: For the first part of this sit, try hard: return to the breath, alert, effortful. Halfway through, set yourself down before God as you know God, perhaps with one quiet name, the way Gajendra lifted his lotus; if you don't pray, set yourself down before the stillness itself. Let the effort soften, and notice what changes.
Or. The small word va in sutra 1.23 that opens a second road: ishvara pranidhana, devotion to the Lord, who meets the devoted one from the other side.

437.title: Yama gives Nachiketa one word
437.hook: a boy turns down every treasure Death offers and gets a single syllable instead; Patanjali tells how to use it
437.carry: japa: say the name, and mean it
437.tomorrow: a king sets out to become a sage, and slips. then what?
437.howItsDone: Many Hindus repeat om or a divine name in japa, often on a mala, a string of beads, and teachers stress that the repetition should be joined with attention to the name's meaning, as Yoga Sutra 1.28 describes.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-THIRTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gajendra's lotus: ishvara pranidhana, a road met from the other side. Today the Lord gets a name.
screen: `ISHVARA PRANIDHANA — MET FROM THE OTHER SIDE.`

segments.voice: You know Nachiketa: the boy who waited three days at Death's door. Yama, lord of death, offers him three wishes to make up for it, and for the third the boy asks what happens after we die. Yama tries to buy him off: long life, herds, gold, music, chariots. Nachiketa says keep them. And in the Katha Upanishad, Death, impressed, begins to teach. Among the first things he gives the boy isn't a treasure at all. It's one word.
screen: `THREE DAYS AT DEATH'S DOOR.` → `GOLD? CHARIOTS? KEEP THEM.` → `ONE WORD INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: Yama says, in paraphrase: the word every Veda praises, the word all austerity is for, the reason students live their disciplined lives, I'll tell you briefly. It is om. This syllable is Brahman; it is the highest. Centuries later Patanjali picks up the same syllable and gives it three sutras, crisp as a recipe. Sutra 1.27: tasya vachakah pranavah. The word that expresses Ishvara, yesterday's Lord, is the pranava, the old name for om. Vyasa adds that the bond between this word and the Lord isn't made up; using the word reveals it. Sutra 1.28: taj japas tad artha bhavanam. Its repetition, and dwelling on its meaning. Japa: saying it again and again. Artha bhavana: letting the meaning soak in as you say it. Sutra 1.29: from that, awareness turns inward and the obstacles fall away. This is the teaching under a practice found in many Hindu homes: japa, a divine name repeated, often on a mala, a string of beads. And the sutra's point is that the sound alone isn't the whole of it. Yama didn't give Nachiketa a noise; he gave him a word with Brahman inside it. Many Hindu teachers say the same holds for any name of God a person loves: Rama, Krishna, Shiva. Today, it's the difference between counting beads while planning your week, and saying the name like you mean it.
screen: `THE WORD ALL THE VEDAS PRAISE: OM.` · `1.27: OM IS HIS NAME.` · `1.28: REPEAT IT, KNOW ITS MEANING.` · `1.29: THE MIND TURNS INWARD.` · then, large: `SAY THE NAME, AND MEAN IT.`

segments.voice: If you have a mala, hold it; if not, use your fingers. On each out-breath, let om sound, aloud or silently: that's japa. After a few rounds, let it carry meaning, the Lord, Brahman, the whole, as you understand it. If om isn't your word, use a name of God you love; if you don't pray, a word for what you hold highest. Again and again, the sound full instead of empty.
Pranava, the old name for om. Sutra 1.27: this word expresses Ishvara. Yama gave it to Nachiketa; Patanjali says repeat it, and dwell on its meaning.

438.title: Vishvamitra slips, and starts again
438.hook: a king sets out to become a great sage and loses his progress to desire, then to anger; Patanjali names the nine obstacles on that road
438.carry: nine obstacles, all part of the path

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-THIRTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: pranava, om, Nachiketa's one word. Japa: say the name, and mean it. Sutra 1.29 promised the obstacles fall away. Today: which obstacles?
screen: `JAPA — SAY THE NAME, AND MEAN IT.`

segments.voice: Vishvamitra starts out as a king who wants a sage's wish-granting cow and can't take it by force. So he gives up his throne to become a sage himself. In the Ramayana's telling, it takes him ages. Brahma names him a royal sage, and he's disappointed; he wanted more. He goes deeper, and the apsara Menaka arrives; ten years pass before he remembers what he came for. He goes deeper still, loses his temper, curses the apsara Rambha, and his hard-won tapas drains away again.
screen: `A KING WANTS TO BE A SAGE.` → `ROYAL SAGE? NOT ENOUGH.` → `TEN YEARS WITH MENAKA. A CURSE IN ANGER.`

segments.voice: Each time, Valmiki says, he sees what happened, grieves it, and goes back to the forest. At last he vows silence, holds back anger altogether, and after a long, fierce tapas Brahma names him a brahmarshi, the highest kind of seer, and his old rival Vasishtha greets him as one. Hindus honor this same Vishvamitra as the seer of the Gayatri mantra, which many say every morning. Patanjali, in sutra 1.30, names what comes in between: the antarayas, nine obstacles. Vyadhi, illness. Styana, dullness. Samshaya, doubt. Pramada, carelessness. Alasya, laziness. Avirati, craving, the pull of the senses. Bhranti darshana, false seeing. Alabdha bhumikatva, not reaching a stage. And anavasthitatva, reaching a stage and not holding it. Vishvamitra's road reads like the last of these: stages reached, lost, and reached again. Sutra 1.31 adds signs in the body that come with them: pain, dejection, trembling, ragged breath. And here is the teaching, plain and very Hindu: the obstacles are expected. The sutras don't treat slipping as proof you're unfit; they name it so you can recognize it and return. The tradition made one of its greatest seers out of a man who slipped again and again. Today, that's a missed week of practice. Not, I'm bad at this. That's illness, or that's number nine, and I'm back.
screen: `HE GOES BACK, AND BECOMES BRAHMARSHI.` · `1.30: WHAT COMES IN BETWEEN.` · `NINE ANTARAYAS.` · `REACHED, LOST, REACHED AGAIN.` · then, large: `THE OBSTACLES ARE EXPECTED.`

segments.voice: Rest on the breath, or on a name of God if you pray, and watch for the nine as they show up: dullness like a heavy fog, doubt asking what's the point, craving with a sudden thought of food or your phone. Each time, name it kindly, there's doubt, and come back, the way Vishvamitra kept going back to the forest. If the breath turns ragged or restless, name that too, and return.
Antaraya, obstacle, literally what comes in between. Patanjali names nine, from illness and doubt to losing a stage you'd reached. Vishvamitra met them, and kept going.

screen: `NINE OBSTACLES, ALL PART OF THE PATH.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana, King Yadu meets a wandering sage, carefree and glowing, and asks where he found his peace. The sage, whom tradition identifies as Dattatreya, says: from twenty-four teachers. The earth, the wind, the ocean, a moth, a honeybee, a python. One of them was an arrow-maker. The sage watched him at work, straightening an arrow, while a king's whole procession went by with all its noise and banners. The arrow-maker never looked up.
screen: `TWENTY-FOUR TEACHERS.` → `ONE OF THEM: AN ARROW-MAKER.` → `A WHOLE PROCESSION. HE NEVER LOOKED UP.`

segments.voice: That, the sage says, is how the mind should rest on the Self: so gathered on one thing that the parade can't pull it away. Patanjali's remedy for the nine obstacles is the same. Sutra 1.32: tat pratishedhartham eka tattva abhyasah. To ward them off, practice on one principle. Eka, one. Tattva, a principle, literally thatness. Abhyasa, the steady return. Which one thing? The commentators part ways. Vyasa reads it as any single object the mind is fixed on; others point back to the sutras on Ishvara and om. Both share a shape: stop spreading out. The obstacles feed on scattering. Doubt grows when you keep switching methods; plateaus feel endless when you keep starting over somewhere new. Vyasa calls the gathered mind ekagra, one-pointed, the ground where real absorption becomes possible. This is the teaching behind a very Hindu habit: keeping one ishta devata, one chosen form of God, and often one mantra received from a teacher, for years, sometimes for life. Not because the other forms are false; Hindus honor many. One is simply where you dig. Today, it's choosing one practice and keeping it long enough to work, while the parade of new apps and new methods goes by.
screen: `THE PARADE CAN'T PULL IT AWAY.` · `EKA TATTVA: ONE PRINCIPLE.` · `OBSTACLES FEED ON SCATTERING.` · `EKAGRA, AND ONE ISHTA DEVATA.` · then, large: `ONE THING, RETURNED TO.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing for this sit: the name of your chosen form of God if you pray, or the breath at the nostrils, or the feel of your hands resting. Each time the mind offers a second thing, a better object, a plan, a new technique, let it pass like the king's procession, and come back to the one you chose. Don't switch, even when something else looks more interesting.
Ekagra, one-pointed, a mind fixed on a single object, like the arrow-maker at his work. Sutra 1.32: to keep the obstacles away, practice on one principle, returning to it again and again.
screen: `EKAGRA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: eka tattva, one thing, returned to. The arrow-maker didn't look up. Day four hundred thirty-nine, done.

440.title: Duryodhana in Maya's hall
440.hook: a prince walks through his cousins' dazzling new hall and leaves burning with envy; sutra 1.33 names the cure he never took
440.carry: friendliness, compassion, gladness, equanimity: the mind clears
440.tomorrow: when baby Hanuman fell, the whole world stopped breathing. why?
440.howItsDone: Many yoga teachers present sutra 1.33 as a daily practice for relationships, consciously meeting the happy with friendliness, the suffering with compassion, the good with gladness and wrongdoers with equanimity.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FORTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: ekagra, the arrow-maker's one-pointed mind. Eka tattva: one thing, returned to. Today, one thing that is a way of meeting people.
screen: `EKA TATTVA: ONE THING, RETURNED TO.`

segments.voice: In the Mahabharata, the Pandava brothers finally have a capital of their own, and the asura architect Maya builds them an assembly hall full of illusions. Their cousin Duryodhana comes to see it. He mistakes a crystal floor for water and lifts his clothes; then he takes real water for crystal and falls in. Bhima laughs out loud. Duryodhana goes home and tells his uncle Shakuni: seeing their good fortune, I'm burning. I can't bear it.
screen: `A HALL FULL OF ILLUSIONS.` → `A FALL INTO THE POOL. LAUGHTER.` → `I'M BURNING. I CAN'T BEAR IT.`

segments.voice: That envy leads to the dice game, and the dice game, in time, to the war. Patanjali names the cure Duryodhana never took. Sutra 1.33 pairs four attitudes with four kinds of people. Maitri, friendliness, toward the happy. Karuna, compassion, toward those who suffer. Mudita, gladness, toward the good. Upeksha, equanimity, toward those who do wrong. Cultivate these, the sutra says, and the mind becomes clear and settled: chitta prasadana, like water once the mud settles. Read the story through it. Duryodhana met his cousins' happiness with envy instead of friendliness, and the laughter with rage instead of equanimity, and his mind never cleared again. Commentators read friendliness toward the happy as the answer to envy: their good news isn't your loss. And equanimity toward wrongdoers isn't approval; it means not letting their wrong take over your mind. Notice the reason the sutra gives. Not only that these are kind, though they are: they keep your own mind clear enough to practice. Buddhists know the same four by another name, the brahma viharas, and practice them too; in the Yoga Sutras, the stated fruit is a settled mind. Today, it's the group chat the moment a friend gets the thing you wanted.
screen: `ENVY, THEN DICE, THEN WAR.` · `FOUR PEOPLE, FOUR ATTITUDES.` · `ENVY INSTEAD OF FRIENDLINESS.` · `EQUANIMITY ISN'T APPROVAL.` · then, large: `THEIR JOY ISN'T YOUR LOSS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone happy right now, maybe someone who got what you wanted, and let a little friendliness rise. Then someone suffering, and let compassion come; then someone who did good, and be glad. Then, gently, someone who did wrong, and let your mind stay level, not agreeing, not boiling. If you pray, hold each one before God for a breath. Then come back to the breath and notice the water.
Friendliness. Maitri, the first of the four attitudes in sutra 1.33, offered to the happy: the thing Duryodhana couldn't find in Maya's hall.
screen: `FRIENDLINESS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: friendliness, compassion, gladness, equanimity, and the mind clears. One for each kind of person. See you tomorrow.

441.title: The day the wind stopped
441.hook: when baby Hanuman is struck down, his father the wind stops moving and the world can't breathe; sutra 1.34 offers the breath as a door
441.carry: prana is life; a slow breath out is a door
441.tomorrow: a man who hated Krishna merges into him. how?
441.howItsDone: Many Hindus begin daily prayer, such as the sandhya, with pranayama, and yoga teachers often introduce sutra 1.34 as a gentle lengthened exhale with a short pause, well before the fuller practices of the second chapter, cautioning students never to strain the breath.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FORTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Duryodhana in Maya's hall: friendliness, compassion, gladness, equanimity, and the mind clears. Today closes the week.
screen: `FOUR ATTITUDES — THE MIND CLEARS.`

segments.voice: As a baby, Hanuman wakes up hungry and sees the rising sun. It looks like a ripe fruit, so he leaps for it. In the Ramayana's telling, Indra, king of the gods, strikes him with the thunderbolt, and the child falls, his jaw broken; hanu means jaw. His father is Vayu, the wind. Vayu picks up his son, carries him into a cave, and stops moving. And everywhere, every creature finds it can't breathe.
screen: `THE SUN LOOKS LIKE A FRUIT.` → `THE THUNDERBOLT. THE FALL.` → `THE WIND STOPS. NO ONE CAN BREATHE.`

segments.voice: The gods rush to Brahma. Brahma goes to the cave and revives the child, the wind moves again, and the gods heap Hanuman with blessings. That's why he's called Pavanputra, son of the wind. The story says what Hindu tradition says everywhere: breath is prana, life itself; when it stops, everything stops. The Chandogya calls breath the eldest and best of the powers, and pranayama, working with the breath, is part of the daily sandhya prayers many Hindus say. Patanjali makes the breath a door for the mind. Sutra 1.34, in paraphrase: or, by breathing out and holding the breath out. Prachchhardana, breathing out; vidharana, keeping it out a while. Notice the va again: or. Not a rule for everyone, one more door in the list that began with the four attitudes. Vyasa reads it as a deliberate breath out through the nostrils and a pause, and calls that holding pranayama, which chapter two takes further. This lesson keeps it gentle: a long breath out, a small pause, nothing strained. Now the week, from the top. Bhagiratha: faith and intensity, not talent. Gajendra: a road met from the other side. Nachiketa's word: say the name, and mean it. Vishvamitra: nine obstacles, all part of the path. The arrow-maker: one thing. Duryodhana: the four attitudes. And today, the wind: the door you always carry.
screen: `PAVANPUTRA: SON OF THE WIND.` · `PRANA IS LIFE.` · `PRACHCHHARDANA: BREATHING OUT.` · `VIDHARANA: A PAUSE, HOLDING OUT.` · `GENTLE, NOT STRAINED.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `THE DOOR YOU ALWAYS CARRY.`

segments.voice: If you pray, begin as many Hindus do before puja, with a quiet name of God. Let the breath be natural for a few rounds, then let each out-breath grow a little longer than the in-breath, slow and easy through the nose, with a moment's rest at the bottom before the next breath comes on its own. No forcing, no gasping; if you feel any strain, go back to normal breathing.
Or. In sutra 1.34, one more door to a clear mind: breathing out, and resting in the pause. Prana, the breath Vayu held back, is the door.
screen: `OR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: prana is life; a slow breath out is a door. Hanuman's father taught the whole world that. That's day four hundred forty-one, and a full week.
